notes.text:
The reproach of Egypt — That is, uncircumcision, was both in truth, and in the opinion of the Jews, a matter of great reproach, and although this was a reproach common to most nations of the world, yet it is particularly called the reproach of Egypt, either,

1. because the other neighbouring nations, being the children of Abraham by the concubines, are supposed to have been circumcised, which the Egyptians at this time were not, as may be gathered from Exod. ii, 6, where they knew the child to be an Hebrew by this mark. Or

2. because they came out of Egypt, and were esteemed to be a sort of Egyptians, Num. xxii, 5, which they justly thought a great reproach; but by their circumcision they were now distinguished from them, and manifested to be another people. Or

3. because many of them lay under this reproach in Egypt, having wickedly neglected this duty there for worldly reasons; and others of them continued in the same shameful condition for many years in the wilderness. Gilgal - That is, rolling.

The passover — Which was their third passover: the first was in Egypt, Exod. xii, 11-24, the second at Mount Sinai, Num. ix, 1-5, the third here; for in their wilderness travels, these and all other sacrifices were neglected, Amos v, 25. While they were in the wilderness, they were denied the comfort of this ordinance, as a farther token of God's displeasure. But now God comforted them again, after the time that he had afflicted them.

Old corn — The corn of the last year, which the inhabitants of those parts had left in their barns, being fled into their strong cities, or other remoter parts. The morrow - That is, on the sixteenth day; for the passover was killed between the two evenings of the fourteenth day, and was eaten in that evening or night, which, according to the Jewish computation, whereby they begin their days at the evening, was a part of the fifteenth day, all which was the feast of the passover; and so the morrow of the sixteenth day, was the morrow after the passover, when they were obliged to offer unto God the first sheaf, and then were allowed to eat of the rest. Parched corn - Of that year's corn. which was most proper for that use. Self-same day - Having an eager desire to enjoy the fruits of the land. And this corn came very seasonably; for after the passover, they were to keep the feast of unleavened bread, which they could not do, when they had nothing but manna to live upon.

The manna ceased — Which God now withheld, to shew that Manna was not an ordinary production of nature, but an extraordinary and special gift of God to supply their necessity. And because God would not be prodigal of his favours, by working miracles where ordinary means were sufficient. The morrow - That is, on the seventeenth day.

glossa.text:
*And they ate,* etc. ((ADAM., hom. 6.)) But when the people went out of the land of Egypt, etc., *as far as* For how is it thought that, the better food ceasing, a worse succeeded.

((JUSTIN., Dialog. )) God in the beginning, before all creatures, begot out of himself a certain rational power, which is also called the Glory of the Lord, and sometimes the Son, Wisdom, Angel, Word, God, Lord. Sometimes also he calls himself the Master of the host, when he appeared in human form to Jesus the son of Nave.

*And he saw a man. ((ADAM., hom. 6 in Josue.))* It came to pass, when Jesus was in Jericho, etc., *as far as* who, having received a kingdom, returned.

notes.text: Imputeth — Whom God doth not charge with the guilt of his sins, but graciously pardons and accepts him in Christ. No guile - Who freely confesses all his sins, and turns from sin to God with all his heart.

Silence — From a full and open confession of my sins. Old - My spirit failed, and the strength of my body decayed. Roaring - Because of the continual horrors of my conscience, and sense of God's wrath.
Hand — Thy afflicting hand. My moisture - Was dried up.
The iniquity — The guilt of my sin.

For this — Upon the encouragement of my example. Found - In an acceptable and seasonable time, while God continues to offer grace and mercy. Waters - In the time of great calamities. Not come - So as to overwhelm him.
I will — This and the next verse seems to be the words of God, whom David brings in as returning this answer to his prayers. Mine eye - So Christ did St. Peter, when he turned and looked upon him.
Will not — Unless they be forced to it by a bit or bridle. And so all the ancient translators understand it.

Sorrows — This is an argument to enforce the foregoing admonition. The Psalmist exhorts the righteous to praise God, for his truth, justice and goodness, ver. 1-5, For creating the world, ver. 6-9. For his providence in governing it, ver. 10-17. For his peculiar favour to his people, encouraging them to trust in him, ver. 18-22.

glossa.text: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,* etc. ((AUG.)) Not those in whom he finds no sin, but those to whom he forgives it. *Iniquities.* He means the tinder of sin, namely concupiscence, etc., *as far as* but that sin may be no more. ((HIERON.)) Iniquities, before faith and baptism: sin, after faith and baptism.

*Blessed is the man.* ((HIERON.)) To whom God forgives, for not of himself. He covers it, that it be not revealed in the judgment; and so it will not be imputed unto punishment. There is no guile in him that accuses himself: he holds in the heart what he confesses here with the mouth.

*Blessed:* because formerly, not confessing to God, I came into sin, while I cried out, if I did any good.

*I was silent.* ((AUG.)) He who will not confess his sins labours without cause in the defence of sins: and since in this he also boasts of his merits, his strength fails the more. ((CASS.)) *Blessed is he to whom he hath not imputed.* To some, who have grievous sins, God imputes them; to others he does not impute them, through mercy, even though they have some — namely to those who do not proclaim themselves just when they are evil, but acknowledging themselves make satisfaction. This I now profess, but formerly: *Because I was silent,* etc. ((AUG.)) Or, *I was silent,* as to sin with my voice, *while I cried out all the day:* while the penalty of sin, or an inward blinding, showed me a sinner, or while my evil life cried out, though I was silent, whether I had done any good.

*While I cried out all the day,* etc. Although a man be not conscious to himself of anything, yet he is not just: for who understands his offences? Whence: *There is a just man that perisheth in his own justice.* And the Apostle: *I am conscious to myself of nothing,* etc.
*The thorn is fastened in.* ((CASS.)) *The thorn,* which lifts up the whole body, that is, pride. ((AUG.)) Likewise *misery,* etc., *as far as: in the hands of a drunken man.*
*My sin.* Diapsalma. Confession, whence pardon, as above the growing old from governance. *I have made known.* ((CASS.)) For *I said* before, etc., *as far as* and God hears.

*For this shall he pray.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. Commending repentance, he says it is common to all the saints; which sundry sects reject, against whom he flees for refuge to God. ((AUG.)) *For this.* Therefore every saint prays, because thou hast forgiven, otherwise he would not be a saint. *In the time,* etc. It is the time of grace, the law, pressing and convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, grace heals. *But yet in the flood,* etc. ((AUG.)) Although the saint pray, etc., *as far as* the saint will pray, saying: *Thou art a refuge. To him.* That is, to God, for he changes the person, as often. They do not draw near who say that fate makes them sin, or fortune, which rules all things, or the people of darkness, which rebels against God.

*I will give thee understanding.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. It is answered to the penitent: *I will give thee understanding,* etc. Behold a psalm of understanding, lest the suppliant be thought neglected, with God for witness. *Thou, deliver.* ((CASS.)) Thou who hast promised, *I will give thee understanding.* Or Christ answers the penitent: A glad end, God gives understanding: whence he exhorts others to the same.

*Become ye not as the horse and the mule,* etc. ((AUG.)) Having received understanding, this penitent turns himself to the proud who defend their sins: therefore you, whom I invite, etc. *The horse,* the untamed Gentile; *the mule,* the Jew slow to believe. ((CASS.)) *The horse,* without discernment of its riders; *the mule,* takes any burdens whatever, etc., *as far as* that is, boasting of one's own strength. *Their jaws.* Or, *the jaws* with which they chew, that is, give victuals more sparingly, that being compelled by necessity they may return. ((AUG.)) Or, thou wilt break them here, and in the world to come there will be many scourges. Or: *Become ye not as the horse,* because there are many scourges here and in the world to come. *Who come not near to thee.* ((CASS.)) For there are those who, if they sin through the weakness of the flesh, do not withdraw from devout prayers.

*Many are the scourges of the sinner,* etc. ((AUG.)) After the bridle, scourges are added for taming, lest he be of those unpunished ones to whom a roving licence of their own way is now given: so this man above said that he was tamed.

notes.text: So that we from this time — That we knew the love of Christ. Know no one - Neither ourselves, nor you, neither the rest of the apostles, Gal. ii, 6, nor any other person. After the flesh - According to his former state, country, descent, nobility, riches, power, wisdom. We fear not the great. We regard not the rich or wise. We account not the least less than ourselves. We consider all, only in order to save all. Who is he that thus knows no one after the flesh? ln what land do these Christians live? Yea, if we have known even Christ after the flesh - So as to love him barely with a natural love, so as to glory in having conversed with him on earth, so as to expect only temporal benefits from him.

Therefore if any one be in Christ — A true believer in him. There is a new creation - Only the power that makes a world can make a Christian. And when he is so created, the old things are passed away - Of their own accord, even as snow in spring. Behold - The present, visible, undeniable change! All things are become new - He has new life, new senses, new faculties, new affections, new appetites, new ideas and conceptions. His whole tenor of action and conversation is new, and he lives, as it were, in a new world. God, men, the whole creation, heaven, earth, and all therein, appear in a new light, and stand related to him in a new manner, since he was created anew in Christ Jesus.
And all these new things are from God, considered under this very notion, as reconciling us — The world, 2 Cor. v, 19, to himself.

Namely — The sum of which is, God - The whole Godhead, but more eminently God the Father. Was in Christ, reconciling the world - Which was before at enmity with God. To himself - So taking away that enmity, which could no otherwise be removed than by the blood of the Son of God.

Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ-we beseech you in Christ's stead — Herein the apostle might appear to some "transported beyond himself." In general he uses a more calm, sedate kind of exhortation, as in the beginning of the next chapter. What unparalleled condescension and divinely tender mercies are displayed in this verse! Did the judge ever beseech a condemned criminal to accept of pardon? Does the creditor ever beseech a ruined debtor to receive an acquittance in full? Yet our almighty Lord, and our eternal Judge, not only vouchsafes to offer these blessings, but invites us, entreats us, and, with the most tender importunity, solicits us, not to reject them.

He made him a sin offering, who knew no sin — A commendation peculiar to Christ. For us - Who knew no righteousness, who were inwardly and outwardly nothing but sin; who must have been consumed by the divine justice, had not this atonement been made for our sins. That we might be made the righteousness of God through him - Might through him be invested with that righteousness, first imputed to us, then implanted in us, which is in every sense the righteousness of God.

glossa.text: *We know no man.* That is, we praise. *According to the flesh.* That is, one seeking his own things, not those which are Christ's: temporal things, not eternal. Nor ought anyone to do this, because although Christ was mortal as I am, whereby I thought him to be a man only, while I was unbelieving: yet now he is immortal, and so we are secure of the reward. If therefore anyone is born again new in Christ, for him mortality has already passed away in hope, and shall pass away, and a new immortality shall be given. Or, if anyone is new, the old law has passed away for him, and he has a new one. *No man not according to the flesh.* He holds the life to come with a hope so sure, as though it were already present: which was fulfilled in Christ rising again, which is not according to the flesh: not but that we shall rise again in the same substance of flesh, but that it will not be in the same quality of corruption, which is signified by the name of flesh. *And if we have known according to the flesh.* Because although, while he was unbelieving, he understood Christ to have been promised in the law according to the flesh, so that he observed the things of the law and commanded them to be kept: yet nevertheless after his conversion he does not now believe it to be so any longer, but the shadow wholly ceases.

*The old things.* Wholly the Old Testament and all things pertaining to the old man, as such. *New things.* There have come the New Testament, and all things of the new man. *The old things.* As the error of idolatry, upon which the knowledge of the one true God has followed.

*God was in Christ.* By this it is understood that the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. There is unity, where there is no diversity: and therefore the one is in the other, because both their image and their likeness is one.
*Be ye reconciled.* We are reconciled by confessing our sins, and by repenting to him who reconciles us to himself.

notes.text: All the publicans — That is, all who were in that place. It seems our Lord was in some town of Galilee of the Gentiles, from whence he afterward went to Jerusalem, chap. xvii, 11.

He spake — Three parables of the same import: for the sheep, the piece of silver, and the lost son, all declare (in direct contrariety to the Pharisees and scribes) in what manner God receiveth sinners.
Give me the part of goods that falleth to me — See the root of all sin! A desire of disposing of ourselves; of independency on God!
He took a journey into a far country — Far from God: God was not in all his thoughts: And squandered away his substance - All the grace he had received.
He began to be in want — All his worldly pleasures failing, he grew conscious of his want of real good.

And he joined himself to a citizen of that country — Either the devil or one of his children, the genuine citizens of that country which is far from God. He sent him to feed swine - He employed him in the base drudgery of sin.
He would fain have filled his belly with the husks — He would fain have satisfied himself with worldly comforts. Vain, fruitless endeavour!
And coming to himself — For till then he was beside himself, as all men are, so long as they are without God in the world.
I will arise and go to my father — How accurately are the first steps of true repentance here pointed out! Against Heaven - Against God.
And he arose and came to his father — The moment he had resolved, he began to execute his resolution. While he was yet a great way off, his father saw him - Returning, starved, naked.
But the father said — Interrupting him before he had finished what he intended to say. So does God frequently cut an earnest confession short by a display of his pardoning love.

Let us be merry — Both here, and wherever else this word occurs, whether in the Old or New Testament, it implies nothing of levity, but a solid, serious, religious, heartfelt joy: indeed this was the ordinary meaning of the word two hundred years ago, when our translation was made.
The elder son seems to represent the Pharisees and scribes, mentioned chap. xv, 2.
Thy father hath killed the fatted calf — Perhaps he mentions this rather than the robe or ring, as having a nearer connection with the music and dancing.
He was angry, and would not go in — How natural to us is this kind of resentment!

Lo, so many years do I serve thee — So he was one of the instances mentioned ver. 7. How admirably therefore does this parable confirm that assertion! Yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends - Perhaps God does not usually give much joy to those who never felt the sorrows of repentance.

Thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine — This suggests a strong reason against murmuring at the indulgence shown to the greatest of sinners. As the father's receiving the younger son did not cause him to disinherit the elder; so God's receiving notorious sinners will be no loss to those who have always served him; neither will he raise these to a state of glory equal to that of those who have always served him, if they have, upon the whole, made a greater progress in inward as well as outward holiness.

This thy brother was dead, and is alive — A thousand of these delicate touches in the inspired writings escape an inattentive reader. In ver. 30, the elder son had unkindly and indecently said, This thy son. The father in his reply mildly reproves him, and tenderly says, This thy brother - Amazing intimation, that the best of men ought to account the worst sinners their brethren still; and should especially remember this relation, when they show any inclination to return. Our Lord in this whole parable shows, not only that the Jews had no cause to murmur at the reception of the Gentiles, (a point which did not at that time so directly fall under consideration, ) but that if the Pharisees were indeed as good as they fancied themselves to be, still they had no reason to murmur at the kind treatment of any sincere penitent. Thus does he condemn them, even on their own principles, and so leaves them without excuse. We have in this parable a lively emblem of the condition and behaviour of sinners in their natural state. Thus, when enriched by the bounty of the great common Father, do they ungratefully run from him, ver. 12. Sensual pleasures are eagerly pursued, till they have squandered away all the grace of God, ver. 13. And while these continue, not a serious thought of God can find a place in their minds. And even when afflictions come upon them, ver. 14, still they will make hard shifts before they will let the grace of God, concurring with his providence, persuade them to think of a return, ver. 15, 16. When they see themselves naked, indigent, and undone, then they recover the exercise of their reason, ver. 17. Then they remember the blessings they have thrown away, and attend to the misery they have incurred. And hereupon they resolve to return to their father, and put the resolution immediately in practice, ver. 18, 19. Behold with wonder and pleasure the gracious reception they find from Divine, injured goodness! When such a prodigal comes to his father, he sees him afar off, ver. 20. He pities, meets, embraces him, and interrupts his acknowledgments with the tokens of his returning favour, ver. 21. He arrays him with the robe of a Redeemer's righteousness, with inward and outward holiness; adorns him with all his sanctifying graces, and honours him with the tokens of adopting love, ver. 22. And all this he does with unutterable delight, in that he who was lost is now found, ver. 23, 24. Let no elder brother murmur at this indulgence, but rather welcome the prodigal back into the family. And let those who have been thus received, wander no more, but emulate the strictest piety of those who for many years have served their heavenly Father, and not transgressed his commandments. And he said also to his disciples - Not only to the scribes and Pharisees to whom he had hitherto been speaking, but to all the younger as well as the elder brethren: to the returning prodigals who were now his disciples. A certain rich man had a steward - Christ here teaches all that are now in favour with God, particularly pardoned penitents, to behave wisely in what is committed to them.

glossa.text: *A certain man.* By the two parables set before, he intimates how greatly he himself with the angels rejoices over the salvation of the penitent. In this third one he not only shows the joy, but also rebukes the murmur of the envious.

*And he said,* etc. As God has no other by whom he may be formed, by whom he is denied, so this man wishes to use his own power, that he may live with none forming him, none ruling him. *Father, give.* The half of the patrimony is given to those who ask, nor is it the fault of the father who gives to the younger. No age is weak in the kingdom of God, nor is faith weighed down by years, unless indeed he who asks has judged himself unfit. If this man had not withdrawn from his father, he would have known no hindrance of age, but having journeyed into a far country he deservedly wastes the patrimony. *And he divided.* To the faithful, by imparting the protection of his grace which they desired: but to the unfaithful, by granting only the natural benefit of native wit, with which they were content.

*Not after many.* Not long after the institution of the human race, it pleased the soul to carry off with it free choice, as a kind of power of its own nature, and to desert him by whom it was founded, trusting in its own strength. And it consumes those strengths the more swiftly, the more it deserts the giver. This is the prodigal life, which loves to pour itself out and to range abroad in outward shows, leaving him who is more inward to it

*And he began.* Because nothing is enough for prodigal pleasure, because pleasure always has a hunger of itself; deservedly therefore is he in want who has left behind the treasures of wisdom and the height of heavenly riches.

*To one of the citizens.* That one of the citizens is he who, being set over earthly concupiscences by the desert of his own depravity, is called the prince of the world. Who sends him into a farm, because he subjects him to the greed of worldly substance. He feeds swine, when he works those things in which unclean spirits rejoice. *That he might feed swine.* The swine is an unclean animal, which delights in filth; so the devil, who is fed in idols with the blood of cattle, and with the death of man himself. He sent him therefore into the farm, that is, made him his own servant, that he might feed swine, sacrificing to him his own soul.

*And he desired.* The food of demons is drunkenness, fornication and the like, which are enticing and provoke to their own use. Nor have the wanton any other care save to fill their belly, *whose god is their belly ((Philip. III))*. But he cannot be satisfied with them, because pleasure always has a hunger of itself. *No man gave unto him.* Because when the devil makes any man his own, he takes no further trouble for an abundance of vices, knowing him to be already dead.

*How many hired servants.* They who with an eye to the reward to come are busy to work worthy things, are refreshed with the daily nourishment of grace from above. But he perishes of hunger who, living outside the father's house, that is, without faith, seeks the blessed life in empty philosophy.

*Father, I have sinned.* Although God knows all things, yet he awaits the voice of confession. Without danger thou mayest disclose what thou knowest is already known: thou hast a cause why Christ should intercede for thee, nor has he died for thee in vain; the Father too has a cause for pardoning, because what the Son wills the Father also wills.

*Make me,* etc. He does not presume to aspire to the affection of a son, who does not doubt that all that is the Father's is his own, but he desires the station of a hired servant, now about to serve for wages, and yet he testifies that he cannot earn even this except by the father's condescension.

 ((AMBR.)) There is a difference between a slave, a hired servant and a son. A slave, etc., *as far as* which after the father's kiss he most nobly disdains.

*But when he was yet a great way off,* etc. Before he understood God, but yet when he was already seeking him dutifully, yet was not yet returning worthy in works, through the Word incarnate he anticipates the son's return. He came to the earth before that man came to the house of confession, not deserting the Word itself, but in the Word condescending as far as our pilgrimage. The arm, that is, the Son, he humbled into the embrace of the one returning. The father fell upon the son's neck, when he laid upon him the light yoke of his own love, and kissed him, that there might be shown what is said elsewhere: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth ((Cant. I))*. Returning, he receives the kiss of charity from the father, when through grace he is made certain of pardon.

*Bring forth quickly,* etc. The first robe, the garment of innocence, in which the first man was founded, but after the fault he knew himself naked, and took a garment of skin, that is, a mortal one. *A ring.* That is, the seal of faith, with which the promises are sealed in the hearts of belie

*In the hand.* That is, in working: that through works faith may shine out, and through faith works may be made firm. *And shoes.* That is, fortify the examples of those before you in the office of preaching, that both the work may be adorned by living well, and the course by preparing for things eternal.

*Bring the calf.* Preach Christ and make known his death, that a man may both believe in his heart, by imitating him who was slain, and receive with his mouth the sacrament of the passion unto amendment.

*And they began to feast.* Not only is the son refreshed for whom the calf was slain, but the father also and his servants, because the refreshment of God and of the saints is the salvation of sinners. And note that after the robe, the ring, the shoe were given, the calf is sacrificed, because unless a man has put on the hope of the first immortality, unless he has fortified his works with the ring of faith, unless he has preached that very faith by confessing it, he cannot take part in the heavenly sacraments.

*Now his son was,* etc. The son, that is, the people of Israel, who had not gone far off to the worship of idols. Neither was he in the house, because he did not penetrate the inward things of the law: in the literal sense, content, working earthly things, awaiting earthly things. This is he who bought a field, and five yoke of oxen, who, pressed by the burden of the law, enjoys earthly senses, and took a wife in the affection of the flesh. *And when he came.* The son draws near to the house when someone among that people, understanding the law spiritually, condemns the labours of servile work, and considers the liberty of the Church. He hears music and a choir, that is, men full of the Spirit preaching the Gospel with concordant voices. He calls one of the servants, when he takes up some one of the prophets to read. And he questions him, while he searches in him what these feasts of the Church may be in which he does not see himself to be.

*He asked.* And now Israel asks why God rejoices in the taking up of the Gentiles, and by reason of envy he does not know the father's will, and stands outside, although he is entreated through heralds.

*Being indignant.* The Jews were indignant and complained, because Jesus feasted with the Gentiles. And still they are indignant at the salvation of the Gentiles and will not go in. But when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in, the father will go out to entreat Israel, when the calling of the Jews shall be made manifest.

*Behold, so many years. ((HIER.))* Following the righteousness of the law, he is not subject to the righteousness of God. For what greater righteousness of God is there than to pardon the penitent?

*Thy commandment,* etc. As though it were not to transgress it, to envy another's salvation, or to boast oneself of one's righteousness.

*Thou hast killed for him the calf.* They confess that Christ has come, but envy wills not to be saved. So it is of the Jew and the Gentile. But generally it can be taken of the just man and the sinner. *He hath devoured his substance,* etc. The harlots are the superstitions of the Gentiles, with whom he squanders his substance who, having left the wedlock of the Word of God, fornicates with the demon in foul greed. *Son, thou art always,* etc. He does not refute him as one lying, but approving his perseverance with himself, and inviting him to the full enjoyment of a mightier exultation. *All that is mine,* etc. In eternal blessedness, both the single things of all and all the things of each single one.

hymns.title: Deck thyself, my soul, with gladness
Be present at our table, Lord
Come to the table of mercy
Gentile or Jew, servant or free
As we gather at your table
Come, let us eat, for now the feast is spread

places.name: Gilgal
places.id: Israelite encampment east of Jericho near the Jordan. Several candidates have been proposed in the plain between Tell es-Sultan and the river; no site has produced decisive evidence.

places.name: Jericho
places.id: Tell es-Sultan, on the western edge of the Jordan Valley c. 10 km NW of the Dead Sea. Excavated by Sellin & Watzinger, Garstang, Kenyon, and most recently by the Italian–Palestinian expedition.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
echoes.note: 'Do not remember the former things... behold, I am doing a new thing' stands directly behind 'the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.' The pairing of forgotten old / heralded new with the demonstrative 'behold' gives high verbal volume and coherence; the new-creation announcement is unmistakably Isaianic second-exodus language.

echoes.text: “For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth; and the former things shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
echoes.note: 'I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered' supplies both the new-creation (kaine ktisis) vocabulary and the 'former things not remembered' formula echoed in 5:17. High coherence: Paul reads being 'in Christ' as participation in Isaiah's promised new creation; strong availability and thematic fit.

echoes.text: “For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me,” says Yahweh, “so your seed and your name shall remain.
echoes.note: 'The new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me'—the enduring new creation reinforces the new-creation motif of 5:17. Recurrence within Isaiah's new-creation cluster (43; 65; 66) strengthens the case that Paul draws on this stream, though 65:17 is the closer verbal match.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'New creation' (kaine ktisis) figurally recalls the original creation account: being in Christ inaugurates a fresh creative act of God. The link is conceptual and faint, mediated through Isaiah's new-creation language rather than direct verbal contact, so it is marked low and contested.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all'—the Servant bearing the sin of others is the template for 'he made him to be sin on our behalf.' High coherence with Paul's vicarious exchange and the wider Servant theology of 2 Corinthians; volume of the substitutionary motif is strong.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand.
echoes.note: The Servant's life is made 'an offering for sin' (asham / LXX 'sin'), precisely the sacrificial-exchange logic of 'made him to be sin... so that we might become the righteousness of God.' The sin-offering wording and the resulting vindication of 'the many' give high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.
echoes.note: 'The righteous one, my servant, shall make many to be accounted righteous' directly anticipates 'so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.' The righteousness-conferred-on-the-many through the Servant's sin-bearing is a tight thematic and lexical match, the climactic Servant echo behind 5:21.

echoes.text: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, even all their sins; and he shall put them on the head of the goat, and shall send him away into the wilderness by the hand of a man who is in readiness. The goat shall carry all their iniquities on himself to a solitary land, and he shall let the goat go in the wilderness.
echoes.note: 'He made him to be sin' draws on the Day of Atonement, where Israel's sins are laid on the offering and borne away. The cultic 'made to be sin/sin offering' (LXX often renders the sin offering simply as 'sin,' hamartia) underlies Paul's paradox. Coherence with the atoning-exchange logic of 5:21 supports the sacrificial allusion.

echoes.text: He shall lay his hand on the head of the goat, and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before Yahweh. It is a sin offering.
echoes.note: The sin offering (hattat / LXX hamartia) is the technical sacrifice 'for sin'; the LXX's use of the same word for both 'sin' and 'sin offering' lets Paul say God made the sinless Christ 'to be sin.' The double sense undergirds the substitutionary exchange, giving medium volume through the shared Greek term.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'bore the sin of many' and was 'numbered with the transgressors,' supporting the one-for-all sin-bearing exchange of 5:21 (and 'one died for all,' 5:14). Recurrence across Isaiah 53 (vv. 6, 10, 11, 12) strengthens the overall Servant-song dependence of the pericope.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The herald announcing peace stands behind Paul's role as 'ambassador' through whom God makes his appeal of reconciliation. The envoy/herald-of-peace motif coheres with the ministry of reconciliation, but the verbal contact is faint, so the echo is marked low.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”
echoes.note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.

echoes.text: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.
echoes.note: The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: While we were still far off, God saw us and ran.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
We squandered the inheritance and came home in rags.
The Father has put a robe around our shoulders.
The calf is killed; the feast is ready.
We were lost, and we are found. Come, let us worship.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: See the father on the road, robe hiked up, running — running while the son is still a long way off.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You who came home rehearsing your apology, you who fed the pigs and dreamed of bread — the arms are already around you.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The best robe, the ring, the sandals, the fatted calf — for this child was dead and is alive again.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So come in from the field, elder and younger alike; the music has started and the table is full.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: While we were far off, the Father ran and threw his arms around us.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
He puts the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our hand.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
We were dead and are alive; come to the feast.
Turn us, O God, and we will return. Amen.
